title: The hypertrophy series: big vs small muscle groups
summary: He argues big muscles should get heavy, high-volume work with longer recovery, while small muscles should be hit more often with less volume. Strength work on big lifts needs rest between sets; isolation for small muscles can be supersetted in giant sets.
claims: Big muscles have a much higher work capacity because they have more muscle fibers
The common belief that small muscles need less frequency and big muscles more is backwards
Punish big muscle groups with lots of intensity and volume and give them more recovery time; hit small muscles more often with less volume
A muscle's ability to keep moving tonnage late in a session scales with its strength: one that moves 1000 lb may drop to 600, one that moves 100 to 60, a gap of hundreds of pounds
The amount of volume a muscle takes is directly correlated with how long it needs to recover
Go hard on squats with PRs and volume until the legs are tired, then give them time; do not repeat it the next day, as squats are mentally and physically taxing
If you do something like 12 sets for rear delts you are probably not using good weight
Small muscles recover faster because their size creates a smaller training need, so they can sometimes be hit again the very next day
Training forearms only once every four days is wrong; train them whenever you can
Small muscles still need progressive overload, scaled to their size
Do not superset heavy knee flexion or hip hinge work; it taxes the cardiovascular system and you need full rest between sets
Superset isolation movements for small muscles freely; giant sets spread tonnage across many small muscles in about the same time as strength work
Many lifters add a little isolation at the same frequency as their compounds, but isolation work needs a higher frequency than that
